learn.title: How big is a type?
learn.body: `sizeof` tells you how many bytes a type or a variable takes. It is worked out when the program is compiled. Knowing sizes matters once you start handling memory yourself, because you must ask for the right number of bytes.

learn.title: Common sizes
learn.body: On the 64-bit platforms this course uses, this prints `1 4 8`, then `8 8`. Sizes can differ on other systems, so use `sizeof` rather than guessing. `%zu` prints a size.

learn.title: sizeof and arrays
learn.body: For an array variable, `sizeof` gives the total bytes. `int nums[10]` is 10 * 4 = 40 bytes. Dividing by the size of one item gives the item count.

learn.title: Counting the items
learn.body: This prints 40, then 10. The trick works only on a real array variable in the same scope, not on a pointer. You will see why soon.
`sizeof` returns the type `size_t`, an unsigned whole number. Print it with `%zu`, not `%d`.

questions.prompt: On the 64-bit platforms used here, how many bytes is an `int`?
`int nums[10];` What is `sizeof nums` in bytes?
`double d[5];` What is `sizeof d` in bytes?
To get the item count of an array, divide `sizeof` the array by \_\_.
questions.explanation: Total bytes divided by bytes per item gives the count.
`size_t` is the type of `sizeof` results and `%zu` prints it.

questions.prompt: Match each type to its size on a 64-bit platform.
questions.explanation: A pointer holds an address, which is 8 bytes on a 64-bit platform.
